analysis.title: The risks reshaping global AI investment (UBS House View - Daily EMEA)
key_insights: NVIDIA shares fell more than 4.3% on Thursday and pulled the Nasdaq down about 0.4%, after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following reports he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, the board has begun a permanent CEO search and appointed Harvey C. Jones as board chair.

UBS says investors are shifting from rewarding spending commitments to assessing monetization, balance sheet strength, capacity utilization and prospective returns. Underlying AI demand remains robust, with accelerating cloud revenue and expanding orders for computing capacity.
UBS forecasts aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026 and USD 1.4tr in 2027.
Key-person risk deserves more attention. Governance and succession planning may matter more alongside earnings growth, since AI equity gains have been concentrated in a narrow group of companies.

UBS believes recent developments reduce the likelihood of an easing in restrictions on advanced AI-chip shipments to China, and scrutiny of where processors are deployed could increase. Reuters reported senior White House officials are discussing pushing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick out amid Congressional criticism of his oversight of chip export controls.
Greater US restrictions could weigh on sales in some overseas markets but would not necessarily change underlying AI demand, as compute capacity remains in short supply.

AI is increasingly a geopolitical issue. Tracking requirements, regulatory scrutiny and supply-chain friction could raise costs and restrict access to some overseas markets, and may spur investment in alternative supply chains and domestic AI capacity.

Positioning: UBS favors financially strong hyperscalers, since tighter future compute capacity could raise the value of existing infrastructure and lower future capex could support free cash flow. Within semiconductors and hardware it stays selective, favoring quality companies with less margin expansion to unwind, defensive tech such as payment networks, and consumer electronics names that could benefit from lower memory costs. For concentrated tech exposure it would consider diversifying across sectors, asset classes and geographies.
The DXY traded above 103, a level not seen in 10 months, as investors price higher US rates. Two-year Treasury yields rose roughly 35 basis points this week, to as high as 4.89%.

NY Fed President John Williams said there is 'still work to do' on 'stubbornly persistent and high' inflation, adding to Fed speakers pointing to more tightening after stronger-than-hoped inflation data earlier this week.

UBS expects at least two further Fed hikes this cycle, with a risk of a faster sequence of quarter-point moves. It favors short- and medium-maturity bonds and is cautious on the longest maturities given fiscal deficits and heavy Treasury issuance. It expects the dollar to stay supported near term and keeps a bearish USD outlook further out.
